name: Zinner syndrome
aliases: seminal vesicle cyst with renal agenesis

clinicalPearls: A rare congenital malformation comprising the triad of a seminal vesicle cyst, ipsilateral renal agenesis or dysplasia, and ejaculatory duct obstruction
It arises from maldevelopment of the distal mesonephric (Wolffian) duct during embryogenesis, which affects both the ureteric bud and the seminal vesicle on the same side
Often silent until early adulthood, when the seminal vesicle cyst enlarges and causes perineal or pelvic pain, painful ejaculation, dysuria, haematospermia, or infertility
It is regarded as the male counterpart of Mayer-Rokitansky-Kuster-Hauser syndrome in females
Pelvic MRI is the investigation of choice, demonstrating the cyst, the absent ipsilateral kidney, and the associated ductal anatomy
It may be discovered incidentally during imaging performed for other reasons or during an infertility evaluation
Management ranges from surveillance of small asymptomatic cysts to aspiration or surgical excision, increasingly by a laparoscopic or robotic approach, for symptomatic lesions
reference.pathophysiology: During embryogenesis the mesonephric (Wolffian) duct gives rise to the ureteric bud and to the seminal vesicle, vas deferens and ejaculatory duct. An insult to the distal mesonephric duct early in gestation disrupts ureteric bud induction of the metanephros, causing ipsilateral renal agenesis, while the maldeveloped duct produces an obstructed, cystically dilated seminal vesicle. The result is the characteristic ipsilateral triad of cyst, absent kidney and ejaculatory duct obstruction.
additionalDifferentials: Isolated seminal vesicle cyst without a renal anomaly
Ejaculatory duct cyst or obstruction from other causes
Cystic pelvic mass of another origin
additionalInvestigations: Pelvic MRI to define the cyst and ejaculatory duct anatomy and to confirm renal agenesis
Abdominal ultrasound or CT to document the absent or dysplastic ipsilateral kidney
Transrectal ultrasound to characterise the seminal vesicle cyst
Semen analysis where fertility is a concern, which may show low volume or oligo/azoospermia
Assessment of renal function given a solitary functioning kidney
Cyst aspiration for cytology or culture if infection or diagnostic doubt arises
redFlags: Infection or abscess formation within the cyst
Obstructive uropathy or any compromise of the solitary functioning kidney
Rapid enlargement or atypical imaging features raising concern for neoplasm
Intractable pain or infertility significantly affecting quality of life
reference.prognosis: The outlook is excellent for small asymptomatic cysts managed conservatively, and symptomatic cases generally do well after aspiration or excision, although fertility depends on the degree of ejaculatory duct obstruction and on contralateral function.
pitfalls: Overlooking the associated renal agenesis and its implications for a solitary kidney
Mistaking a laterally placed seminal vesicle cyst for a midline mullerian or utricle cyst
Attributing symptoms to prostatitis and missing the underlying congenital malformation
Failing to consider the diagnosis in a young man with painful ejaculation and infertility
management: Manage small, asymptomatic seminal vesicle cysts conservatively with surveillance
Treat symptomatic disease by draining or excising the cyst through transrectal or percutaneous aspiration, transurethral resection or deroofing, or laparoscopic or robotic seminal vesiculectomy
Relieve ejaculatory duct obstruction where it causes pain or infertility
Treat cyst infection or epididymitis with appropriate antibiotics
Protect the solitary functioning kidney by monitoring renal function and blood pressure and avoiding nephrotoxic insults
Address fertility with semen analysis and, where obstruction limits natural conception, sperm retrieval and assisted reproductive techniques
Confirm the anatomy and plan treatment with pelvic MRI, and refer to urology, andrology and reproductive services
